sentences.text: She told him when she was fifteen, and she chose the moment badly, which was on the boat, at the sorting table, with a net coming up.

He listened to the whole thing without stopping work, which is his way, and at the end of it he said: "So there's an octopus with a shelf of cups." "Eight shelves." "An octopus," said her uncle, "with eight shelves." He put a fish in the box.
"Iro, they collect.
That is a thing they do.
They pick up shells and stones and bottle tops and they pile them round the den.
There's a word for it.
It's in the books." She said she knew that.
She said she had read the books, which was true; she had read every book about them the library on the island had, which was two.
She said that piling things round a den is not the same as putting all the cups on one shelf and all the shoes on another.
Her uncle worked for a while without answering, which with him is not avoidance; it is the answer being assembled.
"So it likes cups." He said it without any cruelty at all, which made it worse, and he handed her a bucket.
"It doesn't like cups.
There's a plastic beaker next to a bronze one.

It's not liking anything, it's *sorting* —" "For what?" And Iro stopped, because she had no answer, and because the thing her uncle had done was the only useful thing anybody did for her in six years of thinking about it.
*For what.* An octopus that piles shells round a den is doing something with an obvious purpose: it is building a wall.
Every book says so.
The pile is a defence and the animal moves in behind it.
Nothing on those eight shelves was a wall.
She measured it, eventually, at nineteen, with a slate and a pencil, over four dives.
The shelves are set back under an overhang in cracks too shallow to hide in, arranged along a face that faces out.
If you wanted to hide behind that stuff you would have to bring it out and heap it up, which would take about an hour, and would work, and is not what has been done.
The things are set out.
There is a difference between a heap and a display and every human being alive can tell them apart at a glance, and Iro has never met anybody who could say what the difference consists of.

They are set out where a thing swimming past at the level of the ledge would see them, and they are set out in an order, and the order is not one that any octopus has any use for whatsoever — because *what a thing is for* is a fact about people.
A cup is only a cup if you know about drinking.
A compass is a lump of brass unless you know about being lost.
